speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I relied on a number of people to help with this Motion – a "Chindian" woman, a Malay colleague, an Indian Muslim who wears the hijab, a Chinese Special Assistance Plan school graduand, something of a microcosm of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even amongst the few of us, there were heated debates, passionate arguments and some very emotional sharing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And because racial harmony is about people, about relationships, all of us have a part to play and we must do so with sensitivity, responsibility and in good faith.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Edwin Tong said here earlier today, we need a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This unending project of building racial harmony in Singapore is an unending project of engagement, communication and calibration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And these are three thrusts that I will speak on today which are especially relevant, given the recent incidents in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The first thrust, engagement, is about the willingness to reach out, to teach, to understand and to build understanding.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Government bodies have played a big part in this regard and organisations like OnePeople.sg and the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) have done great work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the efforts of Government and Government-related bodies, community groups and leaders also have a role that they can play.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As its President Mr Sarabjeet Singh noted, "Ms Phua demonstrated humility, kindness, curiosity and sincerity, and that is more important to us…and all of us have walked away as better people." Some might say that this is putting the burden of engagement on minorities and minority groups.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I would like to urge my fellow minorities not to see this as a burden but as a unique opportunity to help strengthen our racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Like the YSA has demonstrated, if we all choose to take this up, we will emerge as a kinder, more gracious and more caring Singapore – the new glue that will bind us together that Minister Edwin Tong mentioned on Saturday.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The second thrust, Sir, is communication, which entails having responsible, mature dialogue, a willingness to speak up without fear, to share lived experiences, to propose how we can do things better and an openness to listen.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Communication is about both what we receive and accept and believe and what we put out.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A lot of communication is now done online.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a multiplicity of sources from independent talk shows to analytical Instagram slideshows and confessional websites.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This has enriched discourse but also spread thin the locus of public attention.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, as regards what we receive and accept online, I would urge Singaporeans to be wary of bad actors and opportunists.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Bad actors are malicious characters who seek to sow dissent between our communities and opportunists may not be malicious but they seek to exploit certain incidents for personal gain – perhaps some attention, perhaps a few more likes or a few more clicks.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While they may be hopping onto legitimate concerns, opportunists do not work towards resolution because they want to extract the maximum benefit from the situation and may therefore seek to exacerbate it and prolong it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, of course, does not mean that we should be too quick to label people as bad actors or opportunists.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, for those who raise awareness on real issues and incidents they have encountered, commentators should not turn the tables on them and victim shame or accuse them of inciting racial disharmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think this accords with the law and it is a cruel and unfair way to treat the original poster.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It may also lead to a chilling effect that may prevent future genuine cases from emerging.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, on information that we post, public figures like politicians, community leaders, even influencers and artistes, have a distinct responsibility when posting about race.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The amplifying nature of social media can propel ordinary individuals who raise issues into the national spotlight.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These individuals would then also have to exercise responsibility and, in particular, must be careful about writing large their personal experiences on their whole community.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The recent incident between Ms Sarah Bagharib and the People's Association (PA) is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: PA apologised quickly, as did Member Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Edwin Tong sent his unreserved apology and expressed dismay at the standee being used as a caricature.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I had the impression that PA was quite ready to engage with Ms Bagharib, including on her concerns regarding larger issues she had raised, like the lack of understanding of the Malay culture.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I thought that things took a different turn when Ms Bagharib made a call for feedback before her meeting with the PA and when her statements started looking like they were intended to be on behalf of the whole Malay community and on matters unrelated to the originating incident.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, members of the Malay community did express disagreement with Ms Bagharib's reading of the incident.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One Hanafi Ahmad wrote in The Straits Times Forum that he or she found Ms Bagharib's comments "unsettling".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Former Member of Parliament Zainal Sapari said that the incident was not racist and that the PA was true to its mission of promoting racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Other minority commentators like Mr Devadas Krishnadas opined that "these pinpoint instances should not be used as opportunities to generalise loosely or to appeal or rally minority groups into some coalition of resistance".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But these are an individual's views and experiences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They must be careful about assuming the mantle of a community spokesperson too easily.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If they say, "My view is not just my view but the view of the community; my voice is the voice of the community and I will meet you and discuss with you on this basis", then, I think it is untenable.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But this having been said, it was still an unfortunate outcome and I still hold out hope for an ultimate happy resolution.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Bagharib has since made private the account that she used to first raise this issue and put out her statements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I watched her online interview and I found her articulate and passionate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: She said her motivation of raising this issue was to build a better home for her daughter, which I think that this is the correct spirit, even if her approach could have been different.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope she will not self-cancel and I certainly hope no one attempts to cancel her.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I invite her to return to the marketplace of discourse, even if not with the PA – perhaps, one day with the PA – but generally as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The third thrust of this unending project of building racial harmony is the ongoing calibration of policies, policy positions and the law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How can they be calibrated and what should we expect to be calibrated?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us start with Special Assistance Plan (SAP) schools.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What is it that bugs some people about the SAP schools?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, it is the impression that one of our constituent races, the Chinese, has an entire educational programme unto itself that benefits from state resources.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen comments online in response that, in return, minorities have madrasahs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Madrasahs are religion-based, they are not race-based, and they exist for entirely different purposes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, Sir, there is a fear that SAP school students are an insular Chinese elite, aloof from the other races.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Language and cultural competency grant us a competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, my colleague who studied Higher Chinese, is able to read, draft and negotiate contracts in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This has enabled her to compete with Chinese lawyers in the Chinese market for legal work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As former Member of Parliament Low Thia Khiang said in this House, "the learning of Mandarin should be part of the overall strategy of anchoring Singapore as a Global-Asian node as it will help us to connect to 1.3 billion Chinese" and it is "a tool of soft power".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Will such schools give their graduates a similar edge to compete in, presumably, India or Malaysia?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: India and Malaysia are very different economies and societies as compared to China.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, business is more easily conducted in English in these countries and we also have the common language of the common law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we should avoid a "you have it, therefore I must have it too" approach when looking at ethnic or ethnic-based policies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Each of the communities in Singapore is different and policies must be designed accordingly to take into consideration these differences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The pragmatic purpose of the SAP schools aside, it is, however, a legitimate and valid concern that these students may become an insular lot.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My colleague, a SAP school graduand, told me that not only did she have little exposure to people of other races while schooling, but that she also did not feel any motivation to seek out, engage or befriend them outside of school as they did not feature in her own lived experience.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: She said that she only made friends from other races when she went to University.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This SAP school experience was echoed by one Mr Lee Young Kai in a letter in The Straits Times Forum published just a few hours ago.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: SAP school graduates may be expected to engage China but they are still Singaporean and they are still part of our multi-racial society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He also elaborated on Dunman High School's Diversity and Inclusivity programme, which paired students with peers from other schools, including the madrasahs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Maliki also spoke about such initiatives this afternoon.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These are good programmes and I urge MOE to expand on these programmes, to make them compulsory as far as possible and to ensure that SAP school students have exposure and can build meaningful relationships with all minority groups in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge, Sir, for more transparency on what is being done in this regard.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It has ensured diversity not only in the Parliament but also within political parties.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, in a multi-racial country, the perception of bias in voting along racial lines is as dangerous as the reality.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is too easy for a losing minority candidate to claim that she or he had lost due to race bias.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If so much heat and noise can be generated from an incident involving a standee and, recently, in the news, about a waffle – and I say this without trivialising those incidents – just imagine how much more divisiveness will be generated from claims of racism affecting elections or the electability of a minority candidate?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of this cannot be downplayed and is a uniquely Singaporean feature of our elections.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We must also take care to segmentise criticisms of a political nature from criticisms of the GRC system's function of ensuring minority representation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If there is a political concern about the GRC, then we should raise it as a political criticism.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not throw out the baby with the bathwater.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The next question is whether we will one day see a minority Prime Minister, which has been a long running topic.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The way I see it, Sir, the selection of a candidate to lead a political party to become the Prime Minister is quite obviously a practical decision.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This person must be able to hold the confidence of Singaporeans of all the races and religions in Singapore and must be able to lead the country and, importantly, to win elections.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is, however, quite different from saying that a particular group of Singaporeans may not be ready for a minority Prime Minister, and that a decision should be made based on this group's sentiment.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To quote Minister Wong, "A minority who wants to be Prime Minister should be aware of these attitudes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It does not mean that he or she cannot be Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But these are the realities on the ground".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think this position gives a very timely and needed assurance to Singaporeans of all races.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I would say that the results show that a minority Prime Minister could actually have a chance of leading a party to win the elections and I am encouraged by this.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will help to avoid hardening of views by offenders by building their understanding of other races and cultures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, Sir, we must look at policies and laws as a whole.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we just pluck out individual policies and critique them on their own, of course there will be much to say.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But policies and laws do not exist in vacuo.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The correct approach is to look at the whole, to identify gaps or inconsistencies, and to plug those.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: After describing several positive experiences with people of other races, he wrote and I quote, “I understand the frustration and anger when a lot of people are currently sharing videos that call out racism or racial disharmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But along with that, let’s not forget the good stuff as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in such tumultuous times, it is small episodes that assure us of our togetherness and that we are one people in this nation…United we stand.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Earlier today, my colleagues and I outlined the Government's multi-pronged approach to tackle racism, racial discrimination and also help realise our aspiration of building a society which values people equally, whether Chinese, Malay, Indian and other races, and are bound by their commonalities, and enlarged by their differences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These points are equally relevant to addressing the issues raised by Mr Thomas.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At a recent seminar, Minister Lawrence Wong outlined the Government’s position on how our present harmony is hard-won; a result of careful thought to laws and policies over several decades.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Unlike, for example, the French model of assimilation, we did not set out to achieve harmony by ignoring or eliminating cultural diversity and getting ethnic minority groups to adopt the language and the norms and the attitudes of the majority group.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the contrary, we have worked hard to entrench the interests of our multi-racial groups.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Constitution itself sets out basic obligations on the part of the Government to care for the interests of racial and religious minorities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have long recognised the need to protect both ethnic communities and also bridge them through a set of common values and a common language.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, we have embarked on a unique path as a multi-racial and multicultural society – one that celebrates its ethnic diversity as strength, while having a shared sense of belonging and identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I dare say, Mr Speaker, very few societies around the world have succeeded in ensuring its citizens live harmoniously together, let alone one which has as much diversity as we do in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What we have achieved is something that we can all be very proud of.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we are not complacent, nor do we presume that what we have achieved is perfect or completed, or that we have achieved a steady post-racial state.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Recent incidents, as Mr Thomas has outlined, of racist behaviour that have gone viral remind us there is nothing natural or nothing preordained about our state of racial harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And without due care and attention constantly, the good progress we have made can be lost very quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Thomas has suggested, and I agree, this means that we need to work constantly to ensure our racial harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also have to calibrate our laws, as he has suggested, and policies to ensure that they remain relevant and fair.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Changing social attitudes mean that every generation will of course have to decide its own balance on issues of race and other sensitive issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, our policies are not set in stone, but must be refined to keep pace with societal changes, keeping the overarching raison d'etre as the focus.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I thank Mr Thomas for the suggestions that he has made to calibrate some of our policies.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, as he has pointed out, the core, the essence, of our policies continues to remain relevant today.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As we review our policies, we will engage multiple stakeholders, some of whom who may well have conflicting views.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will endeavour to seek consensus on the changes that we choose to undertake, so that policy change and policy shifts can unite and not divide us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we must also be conscious that what might work in other countries, in other societies, in other jurisdictions, might not work in the same way as our context will be different and we must always remain sensitive to local realities and our own lived experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Shifts in our policy positions will also not come about because of populist sentiments or from who shouts the loudest.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But you can be assured, Mr Speaker, that at the heart of it, the Government will always seek to preserve our hard-earned multi-racial harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, on strengthening our community networks and institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas has emphasised the need to continually reach out and engage diverse groups in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to do so, with the support of community partners to actively promote opportunities to build bonds of trust between races.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the national level, I chair the National Steering Committee on Racial and Religious Harmony or NSC to build close relationships between Government and our ethnic community leaders and also apex religious leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also have the National Integration Council (NIC) to integrate new citizens who may be ethnically similar to us but may come from very different context and different cultural backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the local level, the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) in each of the constituencies foster friendships and build mutual respect at every of these constituency networks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There were also several other initiatives which I have outlined earlier today in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SAP schools, and indeed all schools, should promote social mixing, and meaningful interactions and discourse with students from other communities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Schools will always remain an important common ground to develop cross-cultural understanding and friendships from a young and early age and these will be relationships and mindsets and philosophies that we hope can last a lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, Singapore’s approach to harmony has always been about creating as much common space as possible, working also through the domains of arts, culture and sports – domains that my Ministry is particularly interested in.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, Sir, I think we can do more than just simply bringing people together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We do not want our ethnic communities to just “co-exist” or just “tolerate” each other’s existence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we certainly hope that people can embrace each other’s differences, appreciate that we all have something unique to contribute precisely because we are different, and to stand in solidarity despite our races.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have witnessed many acts of embracement in the past year, as I am sure many Members in this House have, as we stood together as one people especially during the adversities presented by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We want to continue this spirit of embracement, by facilitating and providing opportunities for individuals to join up their different talents for the common good.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the national level, we are expanding opportunities for individuals to partner with the Government to co-create solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Again, not quite respecting strictly the boundaries of race and religion, but looking at the issue as they affect or impact on society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, Sir, nurturing a constructive discourse to build empathy and mutual understanding, a third point that Mr Thomas touched on.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In as much as it is important to expand common spaces, there will also be occasions of differences, discord and disagreement.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will need to be constructive about how this is managed.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Embracing each other’s differences also means being willing to hear from and engage with someone who shares a different view, especially on sensitive matters such as race.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Society falters not when we disagree about things, but when we lose interest in trying to make sense of the other person’s point of view or to understand or to learn and relearn on occasion and trying to engage that person on the merits of our own, to educate, to share and eventually come to a mutual understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas for highlighted the important role of responsible and mature discourse as well, but at the same time, being acutely aware of the need to guard against those who take advantage of and exploit fault lines for their own malicious intent.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Community and religious groups and leaders also play a key role in encouraging constructive discussions, clarifying doubts and misconceptions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And often these doubts and misconceptions are innocent but yet they lie at the heart of some of these insensitivities or misapprehensions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government alone cannot, should not, compel Singaporeans to just have more friends of different races or religions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we can create the conditions and the environment to foster stronger, deeper, more long-lasting harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will convene, we will encourage, we will partner with the community, but I wish to stress that ultimately, connections can only happen when individuals want to make that happen, want to do so and reach out to one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For racial harmony to be enduring, the heavy lifting and the motivation really must come from all Singaporeans, collectively, in an open fashion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Yes, we have to continuously work at forging racial harmony and it is not an easy task.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is really so difficult for many societies to do this well, let alone a racially diverse society like ours.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I urge all Singaporeans from all ethnic communities to engage each other in our commons spaces to forge stronger relations, embrace diversity and also to practise it each day which is important.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And if we can do that, I am sure that our lived experiences will come closer and closer to our aspirations of a truly post-racial society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
